_link.title: I can explain that all cells arise from pre-existing cells and describe the role of mitosis in growth and repair

toLevel2.question: Where do all new cells come from?

options.text: From the division of pre-existing cells
options.explanation: All new cells are produced by the division of pre-existing cells. No cell arises spontaneously.
Cells cannot arise from non-living matter; they are always produced from existing cells.

options.text: From chemical reactions in the environment
options.explanation: Cells are biological structures that arise from cell division, not from environmental chemical reactions.
Protein synthesis occurs within cells but does not create new cells.

toLevel2.question: What are the two main purposes of mitosis in multicellular organisms?

options.explanation: Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells for growth (increasing cell numbers) and repair (replacing damaged or worn-out cells).
Energy production and movement are cell functions, not purposes of mitosis.
Digestion and excretion are organism-level processes, not purposes of cell division.
Mitosis produces genetically identical cells; mutation and evolution are not its purposes.

toLevel2.question: What type of daughter cells does mitosis produce?

options.explanation: Mitosis produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to the parent cell and to each other.
Genetically different cells are produced by meiosis, not mitosis.
Cells with half the DNA are produced by meiosis; mitosis produces cells with the full complement.
DNA is duplicated before mitosis but then divided equally, so daughter cells have the normal amount.

toLevel2.question: How long do stomach lining cells typically last?

options.explanation: Stomach lining cells last only 2-9 days due to the harsh acidic environment and must be constantly replaced by mitosis.
Stomach lining cells have a very short lifespan due to the acidic conditions, not years.

options.text: The entire lifetime of the organism
options.explanation: Only some cells like neurons last a lifetime; stomach lining cells are replaced every few days.
Stomach lining cells last days, not hours.

toLevel2.question: Why are spinal cord injuries difficult to repair?

options.text: Because neurons permanently exit the cell cycle into G0 and cannot divide
options.explanation: Neurons enter G0 permanently, so damaged neurons cannot undergo mitosis to replace themselves.

options.text: Because the spinal cord is too large
options.explanation: Size is not the issue; the inability of neurons to divide is the key challenge.

options.text: Because blood cannot reach the spinal cord
options.explanation: Blood supply is not the main barrier; the permanent G0 state of neurons is the problem.

options.text: Because spinal cord cells divide too quickly
options.explanation: The opposite is true; neurons do not divide at all.

toLevel2.question: Mitosis is responsible for both growth and repair in multicellular organisms.
toLevel2.explanation: Mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells for two purposes: growth (increasing cell numbers) and repair (replacing worn-out or damaged cells).

toLevel2.question: New cells can arise spontaneously without a pre-existing cell.
toLevel2.explanation: All new cells are produced by the division of pre-existing cells. Spontaneous generation of cells does not occur.

toLevel2.question: All new cells are produced by the {{1}} of pre-existing cells.
Mitosis produces {{1}} identical daughter cells for {{2}} and repair.
Neurons permanently exit the cell cycle into {{1}}, which is why spinal cord injuries are difficult to {{2}}.

toLevel3.question: Why is the principle that 'all cells come from pre-existing cells' considered foundational to biology?

options.text: Because it explains how organisms grow, develop and maintain themselves through cell division
options.explanation: This principle underpins our understanding of growth, repair, the cell cycle, stem cells and why damage to certain tissues is permanent.
The principle was established in the 1800s; its importance is its explanatory power, not its recency.

options.text: Because it only applies to humans
options.explanation: This principle applies to all living organisms, not just humans.

options.text: Because it proves cells can form from non-living matter
options.explanation: The principle states the opposite: cells only arise from existing cells.

toLevel3.question: Explain why stomach lining cells need to be replaced so frequently.

options.text: Because the harsh acidic environment damages and destroys them quickly
options.explanation: The stomach's hydrochloric acid environment wears out lining cells within 2-9 days, requiring constant replacement through mitosis.

options.text: Because they are the largest cells in the body
options.explanation: Cell size is not the reason; the acidic environment causes rapid wear.

options.text: Because they undergo meiosis instead of mitosis
options.explanation: Stomach lining cells are replaced by mitosis, not meiosis.
The cells are damaged by the acidic environment rather than choosing to stop functioning.

toLevel3.question: How does the concept that all cells arise from pre-existing cells connect to the importance of stem cells?

options.text: Stem cells are the pre-existing cells that divide to produce new specialised cells for growth and repair
options.explanation: Since all cells must come from existing cells, stem cells serve as the source population that divides and differentiates to maintain tissues.

options.text: Stem cells are the only cells that can die
options.explanation: All cells can die; stem cells are significant because they divide to replace other cells.
Stem cells also come from pre-existing cells; they do not arise spontaneously.

options.text: Stem cells do not undergo mitosis
options.explanation: Stem cells do undergo mitosis; this is how they produce new cells.

toLevel3.question: Why does mitosis need to produce genetically identical daughter cells for effective repair?

options.text: So that replacement cells function exactly like the cells they are replacing
options.explanation: Repair requires cells with identical genetic instructions to maintain proper tissue function. Genetically different cells might not perform the same role.
Different cell types can survive, but repair requires matching cells to maintain tissue function.

options.text: Because the body rejects different cells
options.explanation: While immune rejection is relevant for transplants, the key issue in repair is functional identity.

options.text: Because DNA cannot be copied differently
options.explanation: DNA can acquire mutations, but the purpose of mitosis is to produce identical copies for proper function.

toLevel3.question: Explain the connection between a single fertilised egg and the trillions of cells in an adult human.

options.text: Repeated rounds of mitosis from the original cell produce all the cells in the body
options.explanation: Starting from one fertilised egg, mitosis repeatedly divides cells to produce the trillions of cells that make up an adult organism.

options.text: New cells join the body from the environment
options.explanation: Body cells are produced internally through division, not recruited from the environment.

options.text: The fertilised egg grows larger without dividing
options.explanation: Growth occurs through cell division (increasing cell number), not just increasing cell size.

options.text: Cells are created by chemical reactions in organs
options.explanation: Cells only arise from the division of pre-existing cells, not from chemical reactions.

toLevel3.question: Why is the inability of neurons to divide a significant biological limitation?

options.text: Because damage to neural tissue cannot be repaired through cell replacement
options.explanation: Since neurons are permanently in G0, damage to the brain or spinal cord cannot be repaired by growing new neurons, making injuries devastating.

options.text: Because neurons are not important for the body
options.explanation: Neurons are essential for nervous system function; their inability to divide makes damage especially serious.

options.text: Because other cell types can replace neurons
options.explanation: Other cell types cannot perform the specialised functions of neurons.

options.text: Because neurons are too small to divide
options.explanation: Size is not the reason; neurons are highly specialised and have permanently exited the cell cycle.

toLevel3.question: Growth in multicellular organisms occurs primarily through increasing cell size rather than cell number.
toLevel3.explanation: Growth occurs primarily through increasing cell number via mitosis. While cells may grow during the cell cycle, the main mechanism for organism growth is producing more cells.

toLevel3.question: Stomach lining cells are replaced every 2-9 days because the {{1}} environment damages them, requiring constant {{2}}.
An adult human body contains {{1}} of cells, all produced from a single fertilised egg through repeated {{2}}.
Stem cells are important because they serve as the {{1}} cells that divide to produce new {{2}} cells.

toLevel4.question: A patient suffers a deep cut on their arm. Using your knowledge of mitosis, explain how the wound heals.

options.text: Cells surrounding the wound undergo mitosis to produce new identical cells that fill the damaged area
options.explanation: Mitosis in cells at the wound edge produces genetically identical replacements that gradually fill the gap, restoring the tissue.

options.text: New cells arrive from other parts of the body
options.explanation: While some immune cells migrate to the wound, tissue repair primarily comes from local cells dividing.

options.text: The existing cells stretch to cover the gap
options.explanation: Wound healing requires new cells produced by mitosis, not just stretching of existing cells.

options.text: The wound fills with non-living material
options.explanation: Wound healing produces new living cells through mitosis to replace damaged tissue.

toLevel4.question: A child grows from 50 cm at birth to 170 cm as an adult. Apply the principle of cell division to explain this growth.

options.text: Trillions of new cells were produced through mitosis, increasing the total number of cells in the body
options.explanation: Growth from infancy to adulthood occurs primarily through mitosis producing new cells, increasing the body's cell count.

options.text: The original cells each grew to be 3.4 times larger
options.explanation: Growth is primarily through increased cell number, not just increased cell size.

options.text: New cells were absorbed from food
options.explanation: Cells cannot be absorbed from food; new cells come from division of existing cells.

options.text: The child's DNA expanded to fill more space
options.explanation: DNA size does not change; growth comes from increased cell numbers through mitosis.

toLevel4.question: Compare a tissue that undergoes rapid mitosis (like stomach lining) with one that does not divide (like neurons). Predict which is easier to treat when damaged.

options.text: Stomach lining, because its cells can divide to replace damaged ones
options.explanation: Tissues with active mitosis can self-repair by producing new cells. Neurons in G0 cannot replace themselves, making damage permanent.

options.text: Neurons, because they are more specialised
options.explanation: Greater specialisation actually makes neurons harder to treat because they cannot divide to replace themselves.

options.text: Both are equally easy to treat
options.explanation: Self-renewing tissues heal much more readily than non-dividing tissues.
Self-renewing tissues like stomach lining can heal through natural mitosis.

toLevel4.question: A researcher counts cells in a growing embryo: day 1 has 1 cell, day 2 has 2, day 3 has 4. If this pattern continues, how many cells would be present on day 10?

options.explanation: The cells are doubling each day through mitosis. Day 10 = 2^9 = 512 cells (starting from 1 cell on day 1).
Cells double with each division, not increase by one. The number grows exponentially.
Cell division doubles the number each time, giving exponential growth, not linear.
1024 would be 2^10, but starting from day 1 with 1 cell, day 10 has 2^9 = 512 cells.

toLevel4.question: A lizard loses its tail and regrows it. Apply the principle that all cells come from pre-existing cells to explain this regeneration.

options.text: Cells at the wound site undergo rapid mitosis to produce new tissue that forms the replacement tail
options.explanation: The new tail cells come from division of existing cells at the injury site, consistent with the principle that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

options.text: The tail grows from dead material in the environment
options.explanation: Living cells can only come from existing living cells, not from dead material.

options.text: A completely new tail forms independently of the lizard's body
options.explanation: The new tail grows from existing cells at the wound site through mitosis.

options.text: The old tail reattaches by itself
options.explanation: A new tail is grown through cell division; the old tail is not reattached.

toLevel4.question: A patient has a disease that slows mitosis in their skin cells. Predict how this would affect wound healing.

options.text: Wounds would heal much more slowly because fewer replacement cells are being produced
options.explanation: Wound healing depends on mitosis producing new cells. Slower mitosis means slower production of replacement cells and delayed healing.

options.text: Wounds would heal faster because cells live longer
options.explanation: Slower mitosis means fewer new cells to replace damaged ones, slowing repair.

options.text: Wound healing would not be affected
options.explanation: Wound healing directly depends on mitosis; slowing it would significantly impair repair.
Reduced mitosis would not promote growth; it would impair both growth and repair.

toLevel4.question: An organ donor provides a kidney. The recipient's body uses mitosis for tissue repair after surgery. What cells would mitosis produce at the surgical site?

options.text: Genetically identical copies of the recipient's cells surrounding the wound
options.explanation: Mitosis at the surgical site produces copies of the recipient's own cells, healing the incision with tissue identical to the surrounding area.

options.text: Copies of the donor's kidney cells
options.explanation: Mitosis at the surgical site uses the recipient's own cells as templates, not the donor's cells.

options.text: A mix of donor and recipient cells
options.explanation: Healing at the surgical site involves the recipient's cells dividing to repair the wound.
Mitosis produces identical copies of the parent cells, not new types.

toLevel4.question: Wound healing occurs because cells at the {{1}} undergo mitosis to produce {{2}} replacement cells.
A disease that slows {{1}} in skin cells would result in {{2}} wound healing.
Cell numbers in a growing embryo increase {{1}} because each round of mitosis {{2}} the cell count.

toLevel5.question: Analyse the biological trade-off between neurons entering G0 permanently and the consequence for injury repair.

options.text: Neurons gain extreme specialisation and stability by not dividing, but lose the ability to replace themselves when damaged
options.explanation: The trade-off is between functional specialisation (complex connections that would be disrupted by division) and repair capacity.

options.text: There is no trade-off; neurons simply cannot divide
options.explanation: The permanent G0 state is a consequence of specialisation, representing a biological trade-off between function and repair capacity.

options.text: Neurons benefit from being in G0 with no disadvantages
options.explanation: The clear disadvantage is the inability to repair damage through cell replacement.

options.text: Neurons should always be dividing like skin cells
options.explanation: Dividing neurons would lose their complex connections and specialised functions.

toLevel5.question: Compare the repair capacity of stomach lining cells with neurons. What does this comparison reveal about the relationship between cell division rate and tissue resilience?

options.text: Tissues with high division rates are more resilient to damage because they can rapidly replace damaged cells
options.explanation: Stomach lining cells divide frequently and are highly resilient despite harsh conditions. Neurons do not divide and are extremely vulnerable to permanent damage.

options.text: There is no relationship between division rate and resilience
options.explanation: The comparison clearly shows that division capacity directly affects a tissue's ability to recover from damage.

options.text: Neurons are more resilient because they do not divide
options.explanation: Neurons are less resilient to damage precisely because they cannot divide to replace themselves.
Their resilience differs dramatically due to their different division capacities.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate how the principle that 'all cells arise from pre-existing cells' impacts our approach to treating diseases like quadriplegia.

options.text: It explains why traditional approaches fail and why stem cell research is critical for finding alternative sources of new neurons
options.explanation: Since neurons cannot divide, we cannot rely on natural repair. Stem cell research seeks to provide an external source of new neurons that could replace damaged ones.

options.text: It has no impact on treatment approaches
options.explanation: Understanding that neurons cannot produce new neurons directly shapes treatment strategies.

options.text: It proves that quadriplegia is untreatable
options.explanation: While natural neuron replacement is impossible, the principle guides research toward stem cell-based solutions.

options.text: It suggests we should prevent all cell division
options.explanation: Cell division is essential for life; the challenge is finding ways to replace cells that cannot divide.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why cancer represents a failure of normal mitosis control, viewed through the lens of 'all cells from pre-existing cells.'

options.text: Cancer cells are still pre-existing cells dividing, but without the controls that normally limit when and how often division occurs
options.explanation: Cancer does not violate the principle — cancer cells come from normal cells. The failure is in the regulatory mechanisms that control how often these divisions occur.

options.text: Cancer cells arise spontaneously, violating the principle
options.explanation: Cancer cells always originate from existing body cells that have accumulated mutations in growth control genes.

options.text: Cancer has nothing to do with cell division
options.explanation: Cancer is fundamentally a disease of uncontrolled cell division.

options.text: Cancer cells come from outside the body
options.explanation: Cancer cells originate from the patient's own cells that have lost division control.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why some tissues maintain a population of stem cells while others do not. What does this reveal about tissue function?

options.text: Tissues that experience regular wear maintain stem cells for constant replacement, while stable tissues sacrifice renewal for specialisation
options.explanation: High-turnover tissues like skin and gut lining maintain stem cells because they need constant replacement. Stable tissues like neurons prioritise specialisation over self-renewal.

options.text: All tissues have equal numbers of stem cells
options.explanation: Different tissues have very different stem cell populations based on their renewal needs.

options.text: Stem cells are only found in embryos
options.explanation: Adult stem cells exist in many tissues throughout life, particularly in those requiring regular renewal.

options.text: Tissues without stem cells are less important
options.explanation: Neurons lack stem cells but are critically important; the difference reflects functional needs, not importance.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate the statement: 'If we could reactivate mitosis in neurons, we could cure spinal cord injuries.'

options.text: This is oversimplified — new neurons would need to form correct connections and integrate into existing neural circuits, not just increase in number
options.explanation: Simply producing new neurons is insufficient; they would need to establish the precise connections that enable nervous system function, which is an enormous additional challenge.

options.text: This is completely correct — more neurons would solve the problem
options.explanation: New neurons alone would not restore function without proper connectivity and integration.

options.text: This is impossible because neurons have no DNA
options.explanation: Neurons have DNA; the issue is that they are in G0 and do not divide, not that they lack DNA.

options.text: This is correct because all cells are the same
options.explanation: Neurons are highly specialised cells that require precise connections, making simple cell number replacement insufficient.

toLevel5.question: Analyse how the rate of mitosis in a tissue reflects its exposure to damage.

options.text: Tissues exposed to more damage tend to have higher mitotic rates to maintain cell numbers despite constant cell loss
options.explanation: Stomach lining (high acid exposure, high mitotic rate) and skin (environmental exposure, moderate mitotic rate) demonstrate this relationship between damage exposure and replacement rate.

options.text: Mitotic rate is the same in all tissues
options.explanation: Mitotic rates vary dramatically between tissues based on their renewal needs.

options.text: Tissues with more damage have lower mitotic rates
options.explanation: The opposite is true; higher damage exposure requires higher replacement rates.

options.text: Damage has no effect on mitotic rate
options.explanation: The body's mitotic rates have evolved to match the renewal needs of each tissue type.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate the evolutionary advantage of having some cells permanently exit the cell cycle.

options.text: It allows maximum specialisation for complex functions that would be disrupted by cell division
options.explanation: Neurons and muscle cells need stable, long-term structures (neural connections, sarcomeres). Dividing would disrupt these structures and impair function.
The advantage is clear: highly specialised cells perform complex functions better when they don't divide.

options.text: It saves energy for the organism
options.explanation: While energy savings may occur, the primary advantage is maintaining complex cellular structures essential for specialised function.

options.text: It prevents cancer in those tissues
options.explanation: While non-dividing cells have lower cancer risk, this is a secondary benefit, not the primary evolutionary advantage.

Cancer cells originate from {{1}} cells that have lost {{2}} over cell division.
